study.title: Jeremiah 26 - The prophet in judgment and the faithfulness of God
study.overview: Jeremiah 26 shows the prophet announced in the courtyard of the temple, amidst a public crisis: his message of judgment against Judah and Jerusalem provokes rejection, the threat of death and a judgment before leaders and people. The chapter highlights the tension between the word of God and human reactions: priests and prophets accuse him, the princes evaluate the case, the elders remember examples of the past, and a strong contrast appears between the fate of Uriah and the protection received by Jeremiah. The center of the narrative is that the authority of the prophet does not come from himself, but from the LORD, and that the correct answer would be repentance, not violence against the messenger.

outline.title: The order to proclaim without omitting anything
outline.explanation: At the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, Jeremiah receives the mission to speak in the courtyard of the house of the LORD to all who came to worship. The message is complete and without cuts: if the people do not hear the Law and do not answer the prophets sent by God, the house of the LORD will be like Shiloh and the city will become a curse. The focus is on the real possibility of repentance and suspension of judgment, showing that the divine warning aims to call conversion.

outline.title: Religious reaction and death charge
outline.explanation: When Jeremiah ends, priests, prophets and people grab him and accuse him of dying for having prophesied against the temple and the city. The indignation grows and the case goes up to the princes of Judah, gathered at the entrance of the new door. The conflict is not just political; it touches the honor of the temple and the authority of the one who speaks in the name of God.

outline.title: The defense of Jeremiah and the precedent of Micah
outline.explanation: Jeremiah answers that the LORD sent him and insists that the people should improve his ways, for there is still a chance of mercy. He puts himself in the hands of the present, but warns him that killing him will bring innocent blood over the city. The princes and the people consider him innocent, and the elders remember the case of Micah in the days of Hezekiah: instead of killing the prophet, the king feared the LORD, he prayed, and the evil was warned. Historical memory serves to show that repentance is a wiser response than repression.

outline.title: The fate of Uriah and the protection of Jeremiah
outline.explanation: The chapter ends with the remembrance of Uriah, another prophet who spoke against the city and the land in the same lines of Jeremiah. Jehoakim pursued him, Uriah fled to Egypt, was brought back, and killed by the sword, and cast into a common grave. In contrast, Jeremiah is protected by the hand of Ahhan the son of Shaphan, and is not given over to the people to die, showing that God's providence can use the action of faithful allies to preserve his servant.

study.context: The chapter is at the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah. The text itself shows Jeremiah speaking in the courtyard of the house of the LORD during the meeting of the people in adoration, in a context of strong religious sensitivity. The notes inform that there was a formal judgment of the prophet before priests, prophets, princes, and people. Also appear as reference the Silo disaster, the memory of Micah in the days of Hezekiah and the figure of Ahitã, linked to the period of Josiah. All this is presented by the text as moral and spiritual memory, not as simple historical curiosity.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter teaches that the word of God is sovereign and cannot be reduced, adapted or silent to please the audience. The temple alone does not protect a people who reject the covenant; the presence of the sanctuary does not replace obedience. There is also a principle of moral responsibility: to reject God's envoy is to reject the message of God Himself. At the same time, the text preserves the possibility of real repentance, for the judgment announced is not fatalism; it is a call to change. Jeremiah's defense reinforces that prophetic fidelity can cost suffering, but God can preserve it by human means. The contrast between Micah, Uriah and Jeremiah shows that the same God can allow different outcomes, without which invalidates the truth of the message.

scholarViews.insight: The chapter presents Jeremiah being judged before priests and prophets, because he declared that the Lord would destroy the temple and Jerusalem; the holiness of the temple was in dispute.
The people's reaction to preaching shows that a true message, said in the name of God, can awaken hostility instead of repentance; priests and prophets treat him as a criminal.
Jeremiah states that his commission comes from the Lord and that he did not seek this mission on his own; his authority depends on the divine sending.

questions: What does this chapter teach about the difference between defending religious traditions and obeying the word of God?
Why did the leaders consider Jeremiah guilty, and why did the elders remember Micah's case?
How does the contrast between Uriah and Jeremiah help to understand the cost and protection of the faithful ministry?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to hear the correction of God without hardening the heart. In practice, this means examining habits, words and decisions in the light of Scripture, rather than automatically defending what we already think. It also teaches not to treat faithful messengers as enemies when the message confronts sin or injustice. In community, it is worth cultivating space for repentance, prayer and reviewing ways before resistance to the Lord becomes obstinacy. And if there is opposition by faithfulness to the gospel, the chapter encourages to stand firm, trusting that God can preserve and vindicate his servants.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided allow to safely affirm the focus of Jeremiah's judgment, the role of Ahchaan and the precedent of Micah and Uriah. However, there is not enough basis here to detail beyond the broad political context of Jehoiakim's reign, nor to identify with certainty all the agents mentioned outside the text itself. It is also important to note that Tyndale's readings, Matthew Henry and Adam Clarke are interpretations, not mandatory conclusions of the text.
